claim: Mitotic chromosomes decrease in size during development.
source: Mitotic chromosomes also decrease in size during development, presumably to scale coordinately with mitotic spindles, but the underlying mechanisms are unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known observation that motivates the study.

claim: Mitotic chromosomes scale continuously with cell, spindle, and nuclear size in vivo.
source: We found that mitotic chromosomes scale continuously with cell, spindle, and nuclear size in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-embryo immunofluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mitotic chromosome size cannot be reset by cytoplasmic factors from earlier developmental stages.
source: However, unlike for spindles and nuclei, mitotic chromosome size cannot be reset by cytoplasmic factors from earlier developmental stages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that mixing metaphase-arrested egg extracts with stage 8 mitotic embryo extracts did not increase chromosome length (Figure 2B).

claim: Increasing nuclear-cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio is sufficient to recapitulate mitotic chromosome scaling in vitro.
source: In vitro, increasing nuclear-cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio is sufficient to recapitulate mitotic chromosome scaling, but not nuclear or spindle scaling, through differential loading of maternal factors during interphase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that varying sperm nuclei concentration in egg extracts decreased mitotic chromosome length (Figure 5B).

claim: Importin α scales mitotic chromosomes to cell surface area/volume ratio (SA/V) during metaphase.
source: An additional pathway involving importin α scales mitotic chromosomes to cell surface area/volume ratio (SA/V) during metaphase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that palmostatin treatment (which mimics higher SA/V) decreased chromosome size, and this was rescued by non-palmitoylatable importin α (Figure 6C).

claim: Mitotic chromosomes shrink during embryogenesis through decreased recruitment of condensin I.
source: Finally, single-chromosome immunofluorescence and Hi-C data suggest that mitotic chromosomes shrink during embryogenesis through decreased recruitment of condensin I, resulting in major rearrangements of DNA loop architecture to accommodate the same amount of DNA on a shorter chromosome axis.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing lower condensin I on short embryo chromosomes (Figure 3D) and Hi-C data showing increased DNA loop size in embryo chromosomes (Figure 4C).

claim: Spindle volumes continue to scale at larger cell sizes even when spindle lengths reach a plateau.
source: Although previous work showed that spindle lengths reach a plateau in cells larger than ~200 μm in diameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; Wühr et al., 2008), measurement of spindle volumes by confocal microscopy revealed that spindles continue to scale at larger cell sizes (Figure 1C), consistent with observations that spindle width correlates more robustly with cell volume than spindle length in cultured cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; Kletter et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from confocal microscopy measurements of spindle volumes (Figure 1C) and is consistent with published observations.

claim: The combined volume of all mitotic chromosomes (the metaphase plate) scaled continuously with cell size.
source: The combined volume of all mitotic chromosomes (the metaphase plate) also scaled continuously with cell size (Figure 1D), similar to published work describing nuclear scaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Jevtić and Levy, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from whole-embryo immunofluorescence (Figure 1D) and is consistent with published work on nuclear scaling.

claim: Total mitotic chromosome volume scaled in size remarkably similarly with both spindles and nuclei.
source: We found that total mitotic chromosome volume scaled in size remarkably similarly with both spindles and nuclei (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data showing the relationship between metaphase plate volume and spindle/nuclear volumes when binned by cell size (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).

claim: Nuclei decreased in size approximately 10-fold over early cleavage divisions.
source: However, the decrease in nuclear volume during early development was far greater than for mitotic structures: nuclei decreased in size approximately 10-fold over early cleavage divisions, while metaphase plate and spindle volumes decreased by approximately 3-fold and 2-fold, respectively (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by measurements of nuclear, metaphase plate, and spindle volumes across developmental stages (Figure 1E and F).

claim: Metaphase plate volumes decreased by approximately 3-fold over early cleavage divisions.
source: However, the decrease in nuclear volume during early development was far greater than for mitotic structures: nuclei decreased in size approximately 10-fold over early cleavage divisions, while metaphase plate and spindle volumes decreased by approximately 3-fold and 2-fold, respectively (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by measurements of nuclear, metaphase plate, and spindle volumes across developmental stages (Figure 1E and F).

claim: Spindle volumes decreased by approximately 2-fold over early cleavage divisions.
source: However, the decrease in nuclear volume during early development was far greater than for mitotic structures: nuclei decreased in size approximately 10-fold over early cleavage divisions, while metaphase plate and spindle volumes decreased by approximately 3-fold and 2-fold, respectively (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by measurements of nuclear, metaphase plate, and spindle volumes across developmental stages (Figure 1E and F).

claim: The fold-increase in chromosome compaction as a cell transitions from interphase to metaphase diminishes from 8-fold in early blastula embryos to 1.5-fold in late blastula stages.
source: This comparison suggests that the fold-increase in chromosome compaction as a cell transitions from interphase to metaphase diminishes from 8-fold in early blastula embryos to 1.5-fold in late blastula stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing nuclear volumes (interphase) and metaphase plate volumes (mitosis) across developmental stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).

claim: Median chromosome lengths decreased approximately 2-fold between stage 3 and stage 8.
source: We found that median chromosome lengths decreased approximately 2-fold between stage 3 and stage 8 (Figure 2A and B), while chromosome widths increased only by ~1.2-fold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by measurements of single endogenous mitotic chromosomes from stage 3 and stage 8 embryo extracts (Figure 2A and B).

claim: Chromosome widths increased by approximately 1.2-fold between stage 3 and stage 8.
source: We found that median chromosome lengths decreased approximately 2-fold between stage 3 and stage 8 (Figure 2A and B), while chromosome widths increased only by ~1.2-fold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by measurements of chromosome widths from stage 3 and stage 8 embryo extracts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Shortening of the long axis is the predominant metric underlying the change in mitotic chromosome size during early embryogenesis.
source: These changes were consistent with the magnitude of metaphase plate scaling during this period estimated by whole-embryo immunofluorescence (approximately 2-3-fold, Figure 1D) and demonstrates that shortening of the long axis is the predominant metric underlying the change in mitotic chromosome size during early embryogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the 2-fold decrease in chromosome length to the 1.2-fold increase in width, and consistency with metaphase plate volume changes.

claim: The median length of endogenous stage 3 mitotic chromosomes was not statistically different from that of replicated sperm chromosomes formed in egg extracts.
source: We also observed that the median length of endogenous stage 3 mitotic chromosomes was not statistically different from that of replicated sperm chromosomes formed in egg extracts (Figure 2B), suggesting that replicated sperm chromosomes formed in egg extracts may serve as a proxy for mitotic chromosome size during the earliest cell divisions.
evidence: This is supported by measurements comparing endogenous stage 3 chromosomes to replicated sperm chromosomes in egg extracts (Figure 2B).

claim: Replicated sperm chromosomes formed in egg extracts may serve as a proxy for mitotic chromosome size during the earliest cell divisions.
source: We also observed that the median length of endogenous stage 3 mitotic chromosomes was not statistically different from that of replicated sperm chromosomes formed in egg extracts (Figure 2B), suggesting that replicated sperm chromosomes formed in egg extracts may serve as a proxy for mitotic chromosome size during the earliest cell divisions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that stage 3 chromosomes and replicated sperm chromosomes have similar lengths.

claim: Combining metaphase-arrested egg extracts with stage 8 mitotic embryo extracts did not increase chromosome length.
source: However, we observed no increase in chromosome length, indicating that mitotic chromosome scaling factors are not exchangeable in the cytoplasm during metaphase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that mixing egg and stage 8 extracts 1:1 did not change embryo chromosome length (Figure 2B).

claim: Mitotic chromosome scaling factors are not exchangeable in the cytoplasm during metaphase.
source: However, we observed no increase in chromosome length, indicating that mitotic chromosome scaling factors are not exchangeable in the cytoplasm during metaphase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mixing egg and stage 8 extracts did not change chromosome length.

claim: Sperm chromosomes formed in stage 8 extracts were at least 2-fold longer than endogenous stage 8 chromosomes.
source: In both cases, sperm chromosomes were at least 2-fold longer than the endogenous stage 8 chromosomes (Figure 2D), suggesting that stage 8 metaphase cytoplasm is sufficient to remodel sperm nuclei into mitotic chromosomes, but unable to recapitulate embryo chromosome size.
evidence: This is supported by measurements of chromosome lengths when sperm nuclei (replicated or unreplicated) were added to filtered stage 8 extracts (Figure 2D).

claim: Stage 8 metaphase cytoplasm is sufficient to remodel sperm nuclei into mitotic chromosomes, but unable to recapitulate embryo chromosome size.
source: In both cases, sperm chromosomes were at least 2-fold longer than the endogenous stage 8 chromosomes (Figure 2D), suggesting that stage 8 metaphase cytoplasm is sufficient to remodel sperm nuclei into mitotic chromosomes, but unable to recapitulate embryo chromosome size.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sperm chromosomes formed in stage 8 extracts are longer than endogenous stage 8 chromosomes.

claim: Mitotic chromosome size is predominantly set by factors loaded during interphase that are not readily exchangeable during metaphase.
source: Thus, mitotic chromosome size is predominantly set by factors loaded during interphase that are not readily exchangeable during metaphase, making mitotic chromosome scaling fundamentally distinct from nuclear or spindle size scaling.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple experiments showing that chromosome size cannot be changed by cytoplasmic factors during metaphase but can be changed by factors present during interphase.

claim: Mitotic chromosome scaling is fundamentally distinct from nuclear or spindle size scaling.
source: Thus, mitotic chromosome size is predominantly set by factors loaded during interphase that are not readily exchangeable during metaphase, making mitotic chromosome scaling fundamentally distinct from nuclear or spindle size scaling.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the mechanisms of mitotic chromosome scaling to those of nuclear and spindle scaling.

claim: G2-arrested nuclei isolated from blastula-stage embryos and added to metaphase egg extracts produced mitotic chromosomes approximately 2-fold shorter than replicated sperm chromosomes formed in the same extract.
source: We next confirmed previous results that G2-arrested nuclei isolated from blastula-stage embryos and added to metaphase egg extracts produced mitotic chromosomes approximately 2-fold shorter than replicated sperm chromosomes formed in the same extract (Figure 3A and B; Kieserman and Heald, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing chromosome lengths from stage 8 embryo nuclei and replicated sperm nuclei in egg extracts (Figure 3B), and is consistent with previous work.

claim: Mitotic chromosome size is determined prior to entry into metaphase, likely by chromatin factors loaded during interphase.
source: This finding further supports the idea that mitotic chromosome size is determined prior to entry into metaphase, likely by chromatin factors loaded during interphase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that G2-arrested embryo nuclei produce short chromosomes when added to egg extracts.

claim: A difference in chromosome size was recapitulated in extracts depleted of membranes through ultracentrifugation.
source: A difference in chromosome size was also recapitulated in extracts depleted of membranes through ultracentrifugation, which are incapable of forming spindles but competent for mitotic chromosome assembly, indicating that spindle formation is not required for mitotic chromosome scaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that embryo chromosomes are shorter than sperm chromosomes in clarified extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Spindle formation is not required for mitotic chromosome scaling.
source: A difference in chromosome size was also recapitulated in extracts depleted of membranes through ultracentrifugation, which are incapable of forming spindles but competent for mitotic chromosome assembly, indicating that spindle formation is not required for mitotic chromosome scaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chromosome size differences persist in clarified extracts that cannot form spindles.

claim: The magnitude decrease in chromosome size was diminished in clarified extracts (2-fold in crude egg extracts compared to 1.4-fold in clarified extracts).
source: However, the magnitude decrease in chromosome size was diminished (2-fold in crude egg extracts compared to 1.4-fold in clarified extracts), suggesting that the spindle and/or membrane-associated factors may contribute to the decrease in mitotic chromosome size observed in blastula-stage embryos.
evidence: This is supported by comparing chromosome size differences in crude versus clarified extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The spindle and/or membrane-associated factors may contribute to the decrease in mitotic chromosome size observed in blastula-stage embryos.
source: However, the magnitude decrease in chromosome size was diminished (2-fold in crude egg extracts compared to 1.4-fold in clarified extracts), suggesting that the spindle and/or membrane-associated factors may contribute to the decrease in mitotic chromosome size observed in blastula-stage embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the magnitude of chromosome size difference is reduced in clarified extracts lacking membranes and spindles.

claim: Embryo nuclei were roughly 2-fold larger in diameter than interphase sperm nuclei.
source: We observed that embryo nuclei were roughly 2-fold larger in diameter than interphase sperm nuclei (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), consistent with the doubling of genome size due to the presence of both paternal and maternal genomes in embryo nuclei, suggesting that intranuclear DNA density is comparable between the two sources of nuclei.
evidence: This is supported by measurements of nuclear diameters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Intranuclear DNA density is comparable between embryo nuclei and sperm nuclei.
source: We observed that embryo nuclei were roughly 2-fold larger in diameter than interphase sperm nuclei (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), consistent with the doubling of genome size due to the presence of both paternal and maternal genomes in embryo nuclei, suggesting that intranuclear DNA density is comparable between the two sources of nuclei.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that embryo nuclei are 2-fold larger and contain twice the DNA (diploid vs. haploid).

claim: Mitotic chromosomes formed by adding stage 8 embryo nuclei into egg extracts were 2-fold shorter than those formed from replicated sperm nuclei.
source: Yet, mitotic chromosomes formed by adding stage 8 embryo nuclei into egg extracts were 2-fold shorter than those formed from replicated sperm nuclei (Figure 3B), while mitotic spindles formed with either source of nuclei were barely distinguishable in size (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by measurements of chromosome lengths from embryo and sperm nuclei in egg extracts (Figure 3B).

claim: Mitotic spindles formed with embryo nuclei or sperm nuclei were barely distinguishable in size.
source: Yet, mitotic chromosomes formed by adding stage 8 embryo nuclei into egg extracts were 2-fold shorter than those formed from replicated sperm nuclei (Figure 3B), while mitotic spindles formed with either source of nuclei were barely distinguishable in size (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by measurements of spindle lengths formed with embryo or sperm nuclei (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Neither nuclear size, intranuclear DNA density during interphase, nor spindle size during metaphase determines mitotic chromosome size.
source: These data suggest that neither nuclear size, intranuclear DNA density during interphase, nor spindle size during metaphase determines mitotic chromosome size and further supports the idea that scaling of mitotic spindles, nuclei, and mitotic chromosomes are not necessarily coordinated.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations that embryo and sperm nuclei have different chromosome sizes despite similar DNA density and spindle sizes.

claim: Scaling of mitotic spindles, nuclei, and mitotic chromosomes are not necessarily coordinated.
source: These data suggest that neither nuclear size, intranuclear DNA density during interphase, nor spindle size during metaphase determines mitotic chromosome size and further supports the idea that scaling of mitotic spindles, nuclei, and mitotic chromosomes are not necessarily coordinated.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations that these structures can scale independently of each other.

claim: Mitotic chromosome scaling could be recapitulated by adding embryo nuclei to metaphase-arrested egg extracts, but chromosome morphologies were distinct.
source: Interestingly, although mitotic chromosome scaling could be recapitulated by adding embryo nuclei to metaphase-arrested egg extracts, chromosome morphologies were distinct.
evidence: This is supported by observations comparing chromosome morphologies in embryo extracts versus egg extracts (Figure 2A vs. Figure 3C).

claim: The separation of sister chromatid arms resulting in X-shaped mitotic chromosomes in embryo extracts was not observed when stage 8 embryo nuclei were added to egg extracts.
source: The separation of sister chromatid arms resulting in X-shaped mitotic chromosomes in both stage 3 and stage 8 mitotic embryo extracts (Figure 2A) was not observed when stage 8 embryo nuclei were added to egg extracts as chromosome arms remained tightly associated along their lengths (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by visual comparison of chromosome morphologies in different extract conditions (Figure 2A vs. Figure 3C).

claim: The factors determining mitotic chromosome size remain associated with chromatin in G2-arrested embryo nuclei even when introduced into metaphase egg extracts.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the factors determining mitotic chromosome size remain associated with chromatin in G2-arrested embryo nuclei even when introduced into metaphase egg extracts, while other factors that determine mitotic chromosome morphology do not.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chromosome size is maintained but morphology changes when embryo nuclei are added to egg extracts.

claim: Factors that determine mitotic chromosome morphology do not remain associated with chromatin in G2-arrested embryo nuclei when introduced into metaphase egg extracts.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the factors determining mitotic chromosome size remain associated with chromatin in G2-arrested embryo nuclei even when introduced into metaphase egg extracts, while other factors that determine mitotic chromosome morphology do not.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chromosome morphology changes when embryo nuclei are added to egg extracts.

claim: Short embryo chromosomes contained less condensin I and topo II, but more histone H1.8 relative to long replicated sperm chromosomes.
source: We found that short embryo chromosomes contained less condensin I and topo II, but more histone H1.8 relative to long replicated sperm chromosomes (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements of these proteins on embryo and sperm chromosomes (Figure 3D).

claim: Condensin II is 5-fold less abundant than condensin I in Xenopus egg extract.
source: We also examined condensin II, which is 5-fold less abundant than condensin I in Xenopus egg extract and plays a minor role in setting mitotic chromosome size (Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi and Hirano, 2011), and similarly observed lower levels on embryo chromosomes relative to sperm chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claim: Condensin II plays a minor role in setting mitotic chromosome size.
source: We also examined condensin II, which is 5-fold less abundant than condensin I in Xenopus egg extract and plays a minor role in setting mitotic chromosome size (Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi and Hirano, 2011), and similarly observed lower levels on embryo chromosomes relative to sperm chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claim: Lower levels of condensin II were observed on embryo chromosomes relative to sperm chromosomes.
source: We also examined condensin II, which is 5-fold less abundant than condensin I in Xenopus egg extract and plays a minor role in setting mitotic chromosome size (Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi and Hirano, 2011), and similarly observed lower levels on embryo chromosomes relative to sperm chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).

claim: Depletion of histone H1.8 from egg extracts lengthens mitotic chromosomes.
source: These results are consistent with a study showing that depletion of histone H1.8 from egg extracts lengthens mitotic chromosomes (Maresca et al., 2005) and more recent work showing that histone H1.8 inhibits binding of condensin I and topo II to mitotic chromosomes (Choppakatla et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claim: Histone H1.8 inhibits binding of condensin I and topo II to mitotic chromosomes.
source: These results are consistent with a study showing that depletion of histone H1.8 from egg extracts lengthens mitotic chromosomes (Maresca et al., 2005) and more recent work showing that histone H1.8 inhibits binding of condensin I and topo II to mitotic chromosomes (Choppakatla et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claim: Differential recruitment of condensins, topo II, or histone H1.8 may contribute to mitotic chromosome scaling during embryogenesis.
source: Therefore, differential recruitment of condensins, topo II, or histone H1.8 may contribute to mitotic chromosome scaling during embryogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these proteins are differentially abundant on short versus long chromosomes, and is consistent with published work on their functions.

claim: Short embryo chromosomes can be reset to lengths observed in replicated sperm samples by cycling the mitotic chromosomes through an additional interphase in egg extracts.
source: Our previous work showed that short embryo chromosomes could be reset to lengths observed in replicated sperm samples by cycling the mitotic chromosomes through an additional interphase in egg extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B; Kieserman and Heald, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing chromosome length changes after cycling through interphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B), and is consistent with previous work.

claim: The abundance of condensin I, topo II, and histone H1.8 increased in the second metaphase compared to the first metaphase for embryo chromosomes.
source: To test whether the abundance of candidate scaling factors was affected, we performed immunofluorescence on mitotic embryo chromosomes formed during the first or second metaphase and found that the abundance of all three factors increased in the second metaphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements comparing first and second metaphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C-F).

claim: Condensin I levels increased 2-fold in the second metaphase, returning to levels found on replicated sperm chromosomes.
source: Of the three factors, condensin I levels increased the most (2-fold), returning to levels found on replicated sperm chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C and D).

claim: Condensin I recruitment is not necessarily regulated by H1.8.
source: Our observation that histone H1.8 levels increased slightly after the second metaphase suggests that condensin I recruitment is not necessarily regulated by H1.8, and that condensin I can override the DNA compaction activity of the linker histone to lengthen embryo chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that condensin I increased more than H1.8 in the second metaphase, and chromosomes lengthened.

claim: Condensin I can override the DNA compaction activity of the linker histone to lengthen embryo chromosomes.
source: Our observation that histone H1.8 levels increased slightly after the second metaphase suggests that condensin I recruitment is not necessarily regulated by H1.8, and that condensin I can override the DNA compaction activity of the linker histone to lengthen embryo chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chromosomes lengthen in the second metaphase despite increased H1.8.

claim: Short embryo chromosomes had increased longer-range genomic contacts along their entire length, as evidenced by thickening of the diagonal in Hi-C contact maps.
source: Hi-C contact maps indicated that short embryo chromosomes had increased longer-range genomic contacts along their entire length, as evidenced by thickening of the diagonal (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data showing differences in contact maps between sperm and embryo chromosomes (Figure 4A).

claim: The shape of P(s) for Xenopus mitotic chromosomes was similar to that observed in earlier work on mitotic chromosomes from human, chicken, and Xenopus, and for rod-shaped dinoflagellate chromosomes.
source: The shape of P(s) was similar to that observed in earlier work on mitotic chromosomes from human, chicken, and Xenopus (Choppakatla et al., 2021; Gibcus et al., 2018; Naumova et al., 2013), and for rod-shaped dinoflagellate chromosomes (Nand et al., 2021), indicating the same overall organization of mitotic chromosomes across diverse species.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of P(s) curves to published data from other species.

claim: The same overall organization of mitotic chromosomes exists across diverse species.
source: The shape of P(s) was similar to that observed in earlier work on mitotic chromosomes from human, chicken, and Xenopus (Choppakatla et al., 2021; Gibcus et al., 2018; Naumova et al., 2013), and for rod-shaped dinoflagellate chromosomes (Nand et al., 2021), indicating the same overall organization of mitotic chromosomes across diverse species.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of P(s) curves across species.

claim: The amount of DNA contained within a layer is estimated by the genomic distance at which the derivative of P(s) is at its minimum, which was 10^6 bp for sperm chromosomes compared to ~10^7 bp for embryo chromosomes.
source: Based on this previous work, the amount of DNA contained within a layer is estimated by the genomic distance at which the derivative is at its minimum, which was 106 bp for sperm chromosomes compared to ~107 bp for embryo chromosomes (Figure 4C, gray bar).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the derivative of P(s) from Hi-C data (Figure 4C), interpreted using previous models.

claim: DNA loop size can be estimated from where the derivative of P(s) peaks at smaller genomic distances, which was between 10^4–10^5 bp for sperm chromosomes vs. 10^5–10^6 bp for embryo chromosomes.
source: Within a layer, DNA loop size can be estimated from where the derivative peaks at smaller genomic distances, which was between 104–105 bp for sperm chromosomes vs. 105–106 bp for embryo chromosomes (Figure 4C, orange bar).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the derivative of P(s) from Hi-C data (Figure 4C), interpreted using previous models.

claim: Mitotic chromosomes scale smaller during development through decreased recruitment of condensin I, resulting in larger DNA loops and more DNA per layer.
source: Combined with our immunofluorescence results from Figure 3, these data are consistent with a model in which mitotic chromosomes scale smaller during development through decreased recruitment of condensin I, resulting in larger DNA loops and more DNA per layer, thus accommodating more DNA on a shorter chromosome axis (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is inferred from combining immunofluorescence data showing lower condensin I on embryo chromosomes with Hi-C data showing larger loops and more DNA per layer.

claim: Mimicking increased N/C ratio by adding a higher concentration of sperm nuclei into egg extract decreased mitotic chromosome length approximately 1.3-fold.
source: We found that mimicking increased N/C ratio by adding a higher concentration of sperm nuclei into egg extract decreased mitotic chromosome length ~1.3-fold (Figure 5B), consistent with the decrease in metaphase plate size observed in vivo at the stage of development corresponding to the N/C ratios tested (stages 6–7, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing chromosome lengths at different nuclei concentrations (Figure 5B).

claim: The decrease in chromosome length due to increased N/C ratio was consistent with the decrease in metaphase plate size observed in vivo at stages 6-7.
source: We found that mimicking increased N/C ratio by adding a higher concentration of sperm nuclei into egg extract decreased mitotic chromosome length ~1.3-fold (Figure 5B), consistent with the decrease in metaphase plate size observed in vivo at the stage of development corresponding to the N/C ratios tested (stages 6–7, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by comparing in vitro results to in vivo measurements.

claim: The chromosome size change due to increased N/C ratio was accompanied by an approximately 1.6-fold decrease in condensin I abundance on mitotic chromosomes.
source: This size change was accompanied by an ~1.6-fold decrease in condensin I abundance on mitotic chromosomes (Figure 5C), with less significant changes for histone H1.8 and topo II (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements at different nuclei concentrations (Figure 5C).

claim: The increased N/C ratio did not significantly affect nuclear size.
source: Interestingly, we found that the increased N/C ratio mimicked in this experiment did not significantly affect nuclear size and increased spindle size (Figure 5D and E), suggesting that the N/C ratio is only capable of scaling mitotic chromosome size, but not these other subcellular structures.
evidence: This is supported by measurements of nuclear size at different nuclei concentrations (Figure 5D).

claim: The increased N/C ratio increased spindle size.
source: Interestingly, we found that the increased N/C ratio mimicked in this experiment did not significantly affect nuclear size and increased spindle size (Figure 5D and E), suggesting that the N/C ratio is only capable of scaling mitotic chromosome size, but not these other subcellular structures.
evidence: This is supported by measurements of spindle size at different nuclei concentrations (Figure 5E).

claim: The N/C ratio is only capable of scaling mitotic chromosome size, but not nuclear or spindle size.
source: Interestingly, we found that the increased N/C ratio mimicked in this experiment did not significantly affect nuclear size and increased spindle size (Figure 5D and E), suggesting that the N/C ratio is only capable of scaling mitotic chromosome size, but not these other subcellular structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that N/C ratio affects chromosome size but not nuclear size, and increases rather than decreases spindle size.

claim: Both nuclei and spindles scale to compartment volume through a limiting-component mechanism.
source: Previous work using lipid droplets to encapsulate spindles and nuclei in different sized compartments showed that both structures scale to compartment volume through a limiting-component mechanism (Chen et al., 2019; Good et al., 2013; Leech et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claim: Maternal components do not become size-limiting for spindles and nuclei until later developmental stages.
source: However, the range of N/C ratios (defined again as genome copies per volume cytoplasm) tested here was significantly lower (approximately 10-fold) than in those studies, suggesting that maternal components do not become size-limiting for spindles and nuclei until later developmental stages.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the N/C ratios tested in this study to those in previous studies, and observing that spindles and nuclei did not scale as expected.

claim: The major molecular determinants of mitotic chromosome size are loaded during interphase.
source: Our previous data strongly suggested that the major molecular determinants of mitotic chromosome size are loaded during interphase.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple experiments showing that chromosome size is set during interphase and cannot be changed during metaphase.

claim: Varying the concentration of stage 8 embryo nuclei added to metaphase egg extracts had no effect on mitotic chromosome length.
source: We tested this model further by varying the concentration of stage 8 embryo nuclei added to metaphase egg extracts and observed no difference in mitotic chromosome length (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).

claim: Titration of maternal factors had already occurred in the embryo by the time nuclei were collected at G2.
source: This observation is consistent with the idea that titration of maternal factors had already occurred in the embryo by the time nuclei were collected at G2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that varying embryo nuclei concentration did not affect chromosome size.

claim: When sperm chromosomes were added directly to metaphase egg extracts, there was no effect of N/C ratio on chromosome length.
source: Also, when sperm chromosomes were added directly to metaphase egg extracts, thus skipping the initial round of replication, there was again no effect of N/C ratio on chromosome length (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).

claim: The factors that set mitotic chromosome length as a function of N/C ratio are loaded during interphase, not metaphase.
source: Thus, the factors that set mitotic chromosome length as a function of N/C ratio are loaded during interphase, not metaphase.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that N/C ratio only affects chromosome size when nuclei go through interphase in the extract.

claim: Protein concentrations in embryos did not change over the course of the early cleavage divisions.
source: As predicted, although protein concentrations in embryos did not change over the course of the early cleavage divisions (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A), the levels of all factors found in interphase nuclei decreased as genome copy number increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A).

claim: The levels of condensin I, H3, and histone H1.8 found in interphase nuclei decreased as genome copy number increased.
source: As predicted, although protein concentrations in embryos did not change over the course of the early cleavage divisions (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A), the levels of all factors found in interphase nuclei decreased as genome copy number increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements of nuclei from different developmental stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B).

claim: Maternal factors loaded onto newly synthesized copies of the genome during interphase are titratable.
source: Together these observations confirm that maternal factors loaded onto newly synthesized copies of the genome during interphase are titratable and demonstrate that a higher density of nuclei (increased N/C ratio) is sufficient to shorten mitotic chromosomes, likely by decreasing levels of condensin I.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that protein levels per nucleus decrease as genome copy number increases, and that increasing N/C ratio in vitro decreases chromosome size and condensin I levels.

claim: A higher density of nuclei (increased N/C ratio) is sufficient to shorten mitotic chromosomes, likely by decreasing levels of condensin I.
source: Together these observations confirm that maternal factors loaded onto newly synthesized copies of the genome during interphase are titratable and demonstrate that a higher density of nuclei (increased N/C ratio) is sufficient to shorten mitotic chromosomes, likely by decreasing levels of condensin I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that increasing N/C ratio decreases chromosome size and condensin I levels.

claim: Importin α was previously identified as a factor that coordinately scales nuclei and spindles to cell size.
source: We previously identified importin α as a factor that coordinately scales nuclei and spindles to cell size by regulating nuclear import of lamin proteins and the activity of a microtubule destabilizing protein, respectively (Brownlee and Heald, 2019; Levy and Heald, 2010; Wilbur and Heald, 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Palmitoylation of importin α drives a fraction of the total protein to the cell membrane.
source: Palmitoylation of importin α drives a fraction of the total protein to the cell membrane, where it can no longer bind to and inhibit its nuclear localization sequence (NLS)-containing cargo that regulates spindle size (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated based on previous work.

claim: As cell size decreases during early cleavage divisions, cell surface area/volume (SA/V) increases, causing a larger fraction of importin α to associate with the plasma membrane.
source: As cell size decreases during early cleavage divisions, cell surface area/volume (SA/V) increases, causing a larger fraction of importin α to associate with the plasma membrane, thus releasing more scaling factors into the cytoplasm (Figure 6A; Brownlee and Heald, 2019).
evidence: This is stated based on previous work.

claim: Mitotic chromosome size decreased with palmostatin treatment.
source: We found that mitotic chromosome size decreased with palmostatin treatment and was fully rescued by the addition of purified recombinant importin α that cannot be palmitoylatated (NP importin α), but not by addition of wild-type (WT) importin α (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing chromosome lengths in DMSO, palmostatin, and palmostatin + importin α conditions (Figure 6C).

claim: The decrease in chromosome size due to palmostatin treatment was fully rescued by the addition of non-palmitoylatable importin α, but not by wild-type importin α.
source: We found that mitotic chromosome size decreased with palmostatin treatment and was fully rescued by the addition of purified recombinant importin α that cannot be palmitoylatated (NP importin α), but not by addition of wild-type (WT) importin α (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (Figure 6C).

claim: Palmostatin-treated chromosomes showed increased abundance of histone H1.8, whereas the levels of condensin I and topo II were unchanged.
source: Immunofluorescence of DMSO- or palmostatin-treated chromosomes revealed increased abundance of histone H1.8 on short palmostatin-chromosomes, whereas the levels of condensin I and topo II were unchanged (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence measurements (Figure 6D).

claim: Importin α partitioning scales mitotic chromosomes to cell size by increasing availability of histone H1.8 in the cytoplasm as cell SA/V increases.
source: These data are consistent with our observation that short embryo chromosomes contain more histone H1.8 than long sperm chromosomes (Figure 3D) and suggest a model in which importin α partitioning scales mitotic chromosomes to cell size by increasing availability of histone H1.8 in the cytoplasm as cell SA/V increases.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that palmostatin treatment (mimicking higher SA/V) increases H1.8 on chromosomes and decreases chromosome size.

claim: Palmostatin treatment during metaphase was sufficient to shrink mitotic chromosomes.
source: Interestingly, we found that palmostatin treatment during metaphase was sufficient to shrink mitotic chromosomes, while palmostatin treatment during interphase had no effect on chromosome length (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing chromosome lengths when palmostatin was added during interphase versus metaphase (Figure 6F).

claim: Palmostatin treatment during interphase had no effect on chromosome length.
source: Interestingly, we found that palmostatin treatment during metaphase was sufficient to shrink mitotic chromosomes, while palmostatin treatment during interphase had no effect on chromosome length (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (Figure 6F).

claim: Partitioning of importin α during metaphase scales mitotic chromosomes to spindle and cell size in a condensin I-independent pathway.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that partitioning of importin α during metaphase scales mitotic chromosomes to spindle and cell size in a condensin I-independent pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that palmostatin treatment affects chromosome size during metaphase without changing condensin I levels.

claim: Increasing N/C ratio during interphase is sufficient to scale mitotic chromosomes during the subsequent mitosis through decreased recruitment of condensin I.
source: Our data suggest that increasing N/C ratio during interphase is sufficient to scale mitotic chromosomes during the subsequent mitosis through decreased recruitment of condensin I, resulting in increased DNA loop and layer size and length-wise compaction.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the N/C ratio experiments and Hi-C analysis.

claim: Importin α partitioning additionally scales mitotic chromosomes to spindle and cell size due to changing cell SA/V ratios during metaphase.
source: In metaphase, importin α partitioning additionally scales mitotic chromosomes to spindle and cell size due to changing cell (SA/V) ratios.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the importin α experiments.

claim: Mitotic chromosome size does not necessarily correlate with either spindle or nuclear size in egg extracts.
source: However, in egg extracts, mitotic chromosome size does not necessarily correlate with either spindle or nuclear size.
evidence: This is inferred from observations that embryo and sperm nuclei produce different chromosome sizes despite similar spindle sizes and comparable DNA densities.

claim: When N/C ratio was varied in egg extracts, mitotic chromosomes shrank 1.3-fold while spindle size increased almost 2-fold and nuclear size remained constant.
source: Furthermore, when N/C ratio was varied in egg extracts, mitotic chromosomes shrank 1.3-fold while spindle size increased almost 2-fold and nuclear size remained constant (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from N/C ratio experiments (Figure 5).

claim: The mechanisms regulating the size changes of spindles, nuclei, and mitotic chromosomes are distinct.
source: Together, these data suggest that although spindles, nuclei, and mitotic chromosomes appear to scale coordinately with one another in vivo, the mechanisms regulating their size changes are distinct.
evidence: This is inferred from observations that these structures can scale independently under different experimental conditions.

claim: Both interphase and metaphase phases of the cell cycle contribute to scaling of mitotic chromosomes.
source: Whereas mitotic spindle size and nuclear size are set by factors operating during metaphase and interphase, respectively, we found that both phases of the cell cycle contribute to scaling of mitotic chromosomes.
evidence: This is a summary of findings showing that N/C ratio acts during interphase and importin α acts during metaphase.

claim: Condensin I acts as a scaling factor only in the N/C ratio pathway and not the importin α pathway.
source: Consistent with this temporal separation of developmental cues, we found that condensin I acts as a scaling factor only in the N/C ratio pathway and not the importin α pathway (Figure 5C vs. Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by comparing condensin I levels in N/C ratio experiments (decreased) versus importin α experiments (unchanged).

claim: The NLS-containing cargo that scale mitotic chromosomes cannot freely exchange with other factors in the egg cytoplasm to lengthen short embryo chromosomes.
source: Together, these data suggest that the NLS-containing cargo that scale mitotic chromosomes, unlike cargos that scale nuclei and spindles, cannot freely exchange with other factors in the egg cytoplasm to lengthen short embryo chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mixing embryo chromosomes with egg cytoplasm during metaphase does not change chromosome size.

claim: The N/C ratio pathway that operates during interphase sets mitotic chromosome size within a certain range, but final mitotic chromosome size is set by importin α partitioning during metaphase.
source: We speculate that the N/C ratio pathway that operates during interphase sets mitotic chromosome size within a certain range, but final mitotic chromosome size is set by importin α partitioning during metaphase, ensuring that metaphase plate size scales with spindle size.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the temporal separation of the two pathways.

claim: Mitotic chromosome size must be coordinated with spindle size in order to prevent chromosome mis-segregation.
source: This idea is consistent with an early model that proposed mitotic chromosome size must be coordinated with spindle size in order to prevent chromosome mis-segregation (Schubert and Oud, 1997).
evidence: This is stated based on a published model.

claim: Depleting condensin I by 5-fold decreased chromosome size by almost 2-fold in egg extracts.
source: In egg extracts, depleting condensin I by 5-fold decreased chromosome size by almost 2-fold (Shintomi and Hirano, 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claim: Within the physiologically relevant range of condensin I concentrations present during early embryogenesis, less condensin I correlates with both increased loop size and increased length-wise compaction.
source: Our results suggest that within the physiologically relevant range of condensin I concentrations present during early embryogenesis, less condensin I correlates with both increased loop size and increased length-wise compaction.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and Hi-C data comparing sperm and embryo chromosomes.

claim: Immunodepletion of H1.8 from Xenopus egg extracts decreased condensin I occupancy on sperm mitotic chromosomes, reducing their length.
source: Another recent study showed that immunodepletion of H1.8 from Xenopus egg extracts decreased condensin I occupancy on sperm mitotic chromosomes, reducing their length (Choppakatla et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claim: An increase in condensin I can act independently of linker histone H1.8 to lengthen embryo chromosomes formed in egg extracts.
source: In contrast, we found that an increase in condensin I could act independently of linker histone H1.8 to lengthen embryo chromosomes formed in egg extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), suggesting that condensin I is the major scaling factor for mitotic chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that condensin I increased more than H1.8 when embryo chromosomes were lengthened in the second metaphase.

claim: Condensin I is the major scaling factor for mitotic chromosomes.
source: In contrast, we found that an increase in condensin I could act independently of linker histone H1.8 to lengthen embryo chromosomes formed in egg extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), suggesting that condensin I is the major scaling factor for mitotic chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that condensin I changes correlate most strongly with chromosome size changes.

claim: The interplay between condensin I and H1.8 on mitotic chromosomes is more nuanced in vivo where total protein concentrations are constant during early cleavage divisions.
source: The discrepancy between this study and the previous one suggests that the interplay between condensin I and H1.8 on mitotic chromosomes is more nuanced in vivo where total protein concentrations are constant during early cleavage divisions (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing results to previous studies and considering the in vivo context.

claim: Chromosome size can be modulated by H1.8 alone, without any changes in condensin I abundance.
source: Our importin α data suggest that chromosome size can also be modulated by H1.8 alone, without any changes in condensin I abundance (Figure 6D), suggesting that condensin I is not the only factor determining mitotic chromosome size in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that palmostatin treatment increases H1.8 and decreases chromosome size without changing condensin I levels.

claim: Condensin I is not the only factor determining mitotic chromosome size in vivo.
source: Our importin α data suggest that chromosome size can also be modulated by H1.8 alone, without any changes in condensin I abundance (Figure 6D), suggesting that condensin I is not the only factor determining mitotic chromosome size in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that H1.8 can affect chromosome size independently of condensin I.

claim: Progressive titration of maternal factors such as histone H3 due to increasing N/C ratio plays an important role in regulating the timing of Zygotic Genome Activation (ZGA) in the embryo.
source: Previous work in zebrafish and frogs suggested that progressive titration of maternal factors such as histone H3 due to increasing N/C ratio plays an important role in regulating the timing of Zygotic Genome Activation (ZGA) in the embryo (Amodeo et al., 2015; Joseph et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claim: N/C ratio could be a universal mechanism for regulating chromatin structure across the cell cycle.
source: Together, these results suggest that N/C ratio could be a universal mechanism for regulating chromatin structure across the cell cycle, but for very different functions: transcriptional regulation during interphase and chromosome segregation during metaphase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that N/C ratio affects both ZGA (interphase) and chromosome size (metaphase).

claim: Increasing nuclear import rates during early cleavage divisions triggers ZGA as the genome gains access to key pioneer factors that create open chromatin states permissive for transcription.
source: Two recent studies in Xenopus and zebrafish propose a model in which increasing nuclear import rates during early cleavage divisions triggers ZGA as the genome gains access to key pioneer factors that create open chromatin states permissive for transcription (Nguyen et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated based on recent published work.

claim: Mitotic chromosomes scale to decreasing cell size in Xenopus laevis embryos.
source: During the rapid and reductive cleavage divisions of early embryogenesis, subcellular structures such as the nucleus and mitotic spindle scale to decreasing cell size. Mitotic chromosomes also decrease in size during development, presumably to scale coordinately with mitotic spindles, but the underlying mechanisms are unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the main observation motivating the study.

claim: Mitotic chromosomes scale to cell size across metazoans.
source: Mitotic chromosomes also shrink in size during development and scale with cell size across metazoans (Conklin, 1912; Kramer et al., 2021; Micheli et al., 1993), but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated based on published observations across multiple species.

claim: In plants and fly embryos, fused chromosomes with extended lengths were reported to mis-segregate during mitosis.
source: In plants and in fly embryos, fused chromosomes with extended lengths were reported to mis-segregate during mitosis (Schubert and Oud, 1997; Sullivan et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claim: In budding yeast, an artificially lengthened chromosome was hyper-compacted during anaphase due to Aurora B kinase phosphorylation of substrates including condensin.
source: Similar experiments in budding yeast showed that an artificially lengthened chromosome was hyper-compacted during anaphase due to Aurora B kinase phosphorylation of substrates including condensin, a key regulator of mitotic chromosome condensation and resolution (Neurohr et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claim: In C. elegans, a screen for genes required for segregation of an extra-long, fused chromosome identified CENP-A and topoisomerase II as regulators of holocentric chromosome size.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, a screen for genes required for segregation of an extra-long, fused chromosome identified the centromeric histone CENP-A and topoisomerase II (topo II) as regulators of holocentric chromosome size (Ladouceur et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claim: As cell volume decreases during development, structural components become limiting for spindle and nuclear scaling.
source: As cell volume decreases, structural components become limiting (Good et al., 2013; Hazel et al., 2013; Levy and Heald, 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on published work on spindle and nuclear scaling mechanisms.

claim: Some scaling factors are regulated by importin α, which partitions between the cytoplasm and the cell membrane and serves as a sensor for the cell's surface area to volume ratio.
source: Additionally, some scaling factors are regulated by the nuclear transport factor importin α, which partitions between the cytoplasm and the cell membrane and serves as a sensor for the cell's surface area to volume ratio (Brownlee and Heald, 2019).
evidence: This is stated based on published work.

claim: In C. elegans, mitotic chromosome size correlates positively with cell size and nuclear size and negatively with intranuclear DNA density.
source: Previous studies of mitotic chromosome scaling, performed mainly in C. elegans, revealed that mitotic chromosome size correlates positively with cell size and nuclear size and negatively with intranuclear DNA density, as haploid embryos contain longer mitotic chromosomes than diploids, and knockdown of importin α or the chromatin-bound Ran guanine exchange factor RCC1 decrease both nuclear and mitotic chromosome size (Hara et al., 2013; Ladouceur et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on published work in C. elegans.

claim: Haploid C. elegans embryos contain longer mitotic chromosomes than diploids.
source: Previous studies of mitotic chromosome scaling, performed mainly in C. elegans, revealed that mitotic chromosome size correlates positively with cell size and nuclear size and negatively with intranuclear DNA density, as haploid embryos contain longer mitotic chromosomes than diploids, and knockdown of importin α or the chromatin-bound Ran guanine exchange factor RCC1 decrease both nuclear and mitotic chromosome size (Hara et al., 2013; Ladouceur et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on published work in C. elegans.

claim: Knockdown of importin α or RCC1 decrease both nuclear and mitotic chromosome size in C. elegans.
source: Previous studies of mitotic chromosome scaling, performed mainly in C. elegans, revealed that mitotic chromosome size correlates positively with cell size and nuclear size and negatively with intranuclear DNA density, as haploid embryos contain longer mitotic chromosomes than diploids, and knockdown of importin α or the chromatin-bound Ran guanine exchange factor RCC1 decrease both nuclear and mitotic chromosome size (Hara et al., 2013; Ladouceur et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on published work in C. elegans.

claim: Xenopus laevis egg extracts can reproduce many cellular processes in vitro including mitotic chromosome condensation and individualization.
source: Female frogs produce thousands of eggs that enable isolation of undiluted and cell cycle-synchronized cytoplasm in the form of egg extracts that reproduce many cellular processes in vitro including mitotic chromosome condensation and individualization (Maresca and Heald, 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on published work describing the Xenopus extract system.

claim: Fertilized Xenopus eggs divide synchronously, allowing extracts to be prepared from embryos at different stages of development.
source: In addition, fertilized eggs divide synchronously, allowing extracts to be prepared from embryos at different stages of development.
evidence: This is a known property of Xenopus embryos.

claim: Embryo nuclei added to egg extracts can recapitulate a decrease in mitotic chromosome size during development.
source: Our previous work suggested that embryo nuclei added to egg extracts can recapitulate a decrease in mitotic chromosome size during development (Kieserman and Heald, 2011), but did not uncover underlying scaling mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Reductive divisions that progressively decrease cell size and increase N/C ratio operate during different phases of the cell cycle to reduce chromosome length over the course of development.
source: Finally, we describe how reductive divisions that progressively decrease cell size and increase N/C ratio operate during different phases of the cell cycle to reduce chromosome length over the course of development.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.
